title: Customers pay with 5, 10, or 20 unit notes for a 5 unit item and you start with no change. Determine whether you can give correct change to every customer in order. Explain the greedy strategy, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Lemonade Change (Greedy Change-Making at a Counter)
keyPoints: Track running counts of five-unit and ten-unit notes only because twenty-unit notes are never returned as change.
A five-unit payment needs no change, a ten-unit payment costs one five, and a twenty-unit payment costs fifteen in change.
The greedy rule for a twenty-unit payment is to prefer one ten plus one five over three fives, preserving the scarce five-unit notes.
If the required change cannot be assembled at any step, return false immediately.
The algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because it uses only two counters.
Correctness follows because five-unit notes are strictly more flexible than ten-unit notes for making change.

s1_definition.oneliner: Give change using the largest notes first to hoard the scarce small notes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Lemonade Change** – a greedy problem where a cashier starting with an empty till must decide whether every customer in a queue can receive correct change for a fixed-price item.
- **Note tracking** – only five-unit and ten-unit counts matter because twenty-unit notes are never returned as change.
- **Greedy rule** – when fifteen units of change are needed, prefer giving one ten plus one five over three fives, preserving the more flexible small notes.
- **Immediate failure** – the algorithm returns `false` the instant any required change cannot be formed from available notes.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time for a single scan and O(1) space for two integer counters.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India branch counter, Priya pays a fixed five-unit service fee using whatever note she has. The teller starts the day with an empty cash drawer and must return exact change from notes collected from earlier customers. The teller always hands back the largest notes first so the flexible small notes stay in reserve for future customers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Customer Queue:  [5]  [5]  [5]  [10]  [20]
                  │    │    │     │     │
                  ▼    ▼    ▼     ▼     ▼
Till State:     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                │  Pay=5   │ fives=1  tens=0  change=0  │
                │  Pay=5   │ fives=2  tens=0  change=0  │
                │  Pay=5   │ fives=3  tens=0  change=0  │
                │  Pay=10  │ fives=2  tens=1  change=5  │
                │  Pay=20  │ fives=1  tens=0  change=15 │
                └──────────────────────────────────────┘
                         Result: true (all served)

Greedy Decision for 20-unit payment (needs 15 change):

  Option A (preferred):     Option B (fallback):
  ┌─────────┐               ┌─────────┐
  │ 10 + 5  │  saves fives  │ 5+5+5   │  wastes fives
  └─────────┘               └─────────┘
       │                         │
       ▼                         ▼
  Fives preserved           Fives depleted
  for future 10s            future 10s may fail
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Lemonade Change is a greedy problem where the key insight is that not all notes are equally useful. I track running counts of the five-unit and ten-unit notes I hold, and I ignore the twenty-unit notes for change because they are never handed back. A five-unit payment needs no change, a ten-unit payment needs a single five, and a twenty-unit payment needs fifteen, which I can make either as a ten plus a five or as three fives.

The greedy decision that makes this correct is to always prefer giving a ten plus a five over three fives when I owe fifteen. Fives are the scarce, flexible currency because every ten-unit payment consumes one, so I hoard them by spending larger notes first. This is provably optimal through an exchange argument: if any valid solution used three fives where a ten-plus-five was available, we could swap without reducing the number of customers served.

The algorithm makes a single pass through the customer queue using only two integer counters, giving O(n) time and O(1) space. Edge cases include an empty queue (trivially true), a queue starting with a ten or twenty (immediate failure), and sequences that barely fail when the last customer drains all remaining fives.

At the National Bank of India, I used this exact logic at a branch counter for a fixed-fee service where the till started empty and had to return exact change to customers in arrival order. The greedy check confirmed whether a given arrival sequence could be fully served and alerted staff before a change shortage occurred.

Remember one sentence: prefer spending the least flexible resource first, so for fifteen units of change, give a ten plus a five before giving three fives.
